title: Short Stuff: The Body in the Cylinder
summary: Short Stuff episode on "the Body in the Cylinder," a mystery from Liverpool. During WWII Blitz-era rubble clearing in 1930s-era Liverpool (the transcript says 1993 and 1945 in places; hosts reference the discovery around the early 1900s era cleanup), a steel cylinder near Great Homer Street was left in place and used as a bench and play object by local children. A boy, Tommy Lawless (later Ringo Starr), spotted a skeletal foot inside, and police and detectives opened it, finding a Victorian-dressed skeleton of a man about six feet tall, a brick wrapped in burlap as a pillow, and papers including a receipt and account sheets for T.C. Williams and Company. Other items included a railway notice, a postcard, and illegible diaries. Investigators considered and rejected the idea that the body was a recent death or that it was T.C. Williams's son, whose body was found accounted for. The cylinder was found to be part of a ventilation shaft. The case was closed around 1947 with no definitive identification; the prevailing theory is that Thomas Kreegan Williams, owner of a paint manufacturing plant, vanished after its ruin and possibly died by suicide. The hosts credit the blog Passing Strangeness for the account and note an earlier Internet Roundup covered it.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the Short Stuff episode with banter about a recording disruption caused by Jerry being muted on a call.

segments.title: Blitz bombing and the steel cylinder
segments.summary: The hosts describe the German Blitz bombing of England, with Liverpool heavily hit. After the bombing, American soldiers clearing rubble near Great Homer Street found a steel cylinder about seven feet long and under two feet in diameter. It was left in place and became a neighborhood fixture where people sat and children played.

segments.title: Discovery of the skeletal foot
segments.summary: Around 1993, one end of the cylinder had loosened enough for a boy, Tommy Lawless, to see a skeletal foot. He told a local cop, Robert Bailey, who brought in detectives and the mystery began.

segments.title: Opening the cylinder
segments.summary: Investigators had a welder open the cylinder. Inside was a Victorian-dressed skeleton of a man about six feet tall with some hair still on the skull, and a brick wrapped in burlap as a pillow.

segments.title: Items found with the body
segments.summary: The cylinder held a London and North Western Railway notice, a postcard from Birmingham, illegible diaries, and papers under the body including a receipt and account sheets for T.C. Williams and Company. The papers were preserved from grave wax that had dripped onto them.

segments.title: Theories and the case closing
segments.summary: The skull was damaged, likely from bulldozing. The coroner first suggested a recent death, which the hosts dismiss. Investigators checked whether it was T.C. Williams's son, but the son's body was accounted for, while the father, owner of a paint plant, had vanished. The cylinder was part of a ventilation shaft. The case was closed around 1947 with the prevailing theory that Williams died by suicide, though others suggested murder or a staged death.

segments.title: Credits and sources
segments.summary: The hosts credit the Passing Strangeness blog, note an earlier Internet Roundup covered the story, and close the episode.
